h1: Crane Hook Inspection and Lifting Equipment Magnetic Particle Testing
html:
Crane hook inspection and lifting equipment NDT with magnetic particle testing looks for cracks in hooks, shackles, eye bolts, padeyes, lifting lugs, spreader bars, sheaves and pins that visual checks can miss. Atlantis NDT travels to your site anywhere in the United States, examines the steel parts you identify, and reports every indication with its location and length. Your owner program or qualified person decides whether the item stays in service. To start, request a lifting equipment MPI quote.

What gets examined and why cracks matter

Lifting hardware fails suddenly when a fatigue crack grows to critical size, and the first stage of that crack is often tight, short and under a layer of paint or grime. Magnetic particle inspection is a common NDT choice for load-bearing forged and fabricated steel because it highlights surface cracks quickly. Parts we are asked to examine include:

  • Crane hooks, especially the shank, the saddle of the bowl, and the threaded or collar area where stress concentrates.
  • Shackle bodies and pins, eye bolts and swivel hoist rings, particularly at the thread root and under the head.
  • Padeyes and lifting lugs welded to structures, vessels and equipment, including the toe of the attachment weld.
  • Spreader bars, lifting beams and other below-the-hook devices, with attention to welds, pin bores and lift points.
  • Crane sheaves, hook block side plates, pins and trunnions on mobile, overhead and gantry cranes.

These parts see cyclic loading, shock loads, side loading and corrosion. Common damage includes fatigue cracks at stress risers, cracks at weld toes, stress corrosion in some environments, and hairline cracks after an overload or hard impact. MT shows these clearly when the part is clean and the field direction is right.

What the standards say and what they do not

Several US consensus standards and federal rules govern lifting equipment, and it helps to be exact about what they require:

  • ASME B30.10 covers hooks, and it requires periodic inspection with criteria such as cracks, deformation and wear.
  • ASME B30.26 addresses rigging hardware such as shackles, eye bolts and turnbuckles.
  • ASME B30.20 and ASME BTH-1 cover below-the-hook lifting devices, including design factors and inspection.
  • OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179 (overhead and gantry cranes), 1910.184 (slings) and 1926 Subpart CC (cranes in construction) set the federal inspection duties.

These documents call for frequent and periodic inspection by a qualified person. They do not all say that magnetic particle testing is mandatory in every case. How often NDT is used, and on which parts, is set by the owner's inspection program, the equipment manufacturer's instructions, or a qualified person's evaluation. Many owners add MT to a periodic or post-incident program and to load-test or heavy-lift preparation, and our role is to perform that examination to the owner's specification and report what it finds.

What MT does and does not measure

Magnetic particle testing finds surface-breaking and near-surface linear indications in ferromagnetic steel. It does not measure the hook's throat opening, twist, or wear on the bowl and shank, because those are visual and dimensional checks that the owner's inspector or qualified person performs with gauges. It does not measure remaining capacity either. A hook with a hairline crack, no change in throat opening and good visual condition should still be taken out of service according to the owner's criteria; that decision belongs to the owner or qualified person, who often follows the standard's guidance that cracks are cause for rejection.

Non-magnetic parts, such as stainless steel hardware, are not suitable for MT; liquid penetrant is the alternative, and our liquid penetrant testing page covers that service.

Technique for hooks, shackles and lugs

The work follows Article 7 principles and ASTM E709, tailored by a written procedure. A typical approach is:

  1. Identify and tag. We record the part ID, rated capacity, manufacturer and any heat or serial markings, and photograph the item before cleaning.
  2. Clean to bare metal where the procedure requires it. Grease, rust scale and thick paint block particles. Cleaning removes loose coating without gouging the surface or masking a crack.
  3. Magnetize in two directions. A handheld yoke or a coil, depending on the part, produces a field across the area of interest. Hook shanks and bowls are examined longitudinally and circumferentially so cracks with any orientation show.
  4. Apply particles. Wet fluorescent particles give high sensitivity on forged hooks and pins; visible particles suit rough outdoor work. Light levels are measured and recorded.
  5. Interpret and mark. Linear indications are separated from non-relevant ones, such as those at a sharp geometric change or a magnetic writing mark, then measured and marked for the owner.
  6. Demagnetize and clean. Hooks and hardware are demagnetized when the procedure requires, so the residual field does not attract ferrous debris, and the surface is cleaned for return to service.

Pin bores, threads and underside surfaces need extra access. Where a part must be removed from a block or rigging assembly, the owner's rigging crew handles disassembly, and we examine it on a bench or work table.

Welded padeyes, lugs and spreader beams

Welded lifting points are attachment welds on equipment that was not necessarily designed for repeated lifting. We examine the toes of fillet and groove welds, the edges of the lug plate and the area around the hole where bearing stress is highest. Because weld inspection standards such as AWS D1.1 govern the fabrication of many lifting lugs, we report to the criteria your engineer names. Our magnetic particle weld inspection page explains the weld-specific technique, and the weld inspection hub shows how MT pairs with visual and ultrasonic work on the same assembly.

Post-incident, overload and heavy-lift preparation

Beyond routine periodic programs, three situations commonly lead owners to call for magnetic particle examination of lifting gear. After a suspected overload, a two-block event, a dropped load or a hard side impact, hooks and shackles may carry cracks that are not visible, and the owner wants a baseline before returning the gear to the line. Before a critical or heavy lift, such as setting a vessel or a transformer, the rigging plan may call for examination of the hooks, shackles, lugs and spreader bars that will carry the load. And on second-hand or inherited equipment with no inspection history, an MT survey of the load path gives the new owner a record to start from.

In each case the scope is the load path: every component the lift force passes through, from the hook block to the attachment on the load. Listing those items in the quote request lets us plan the number of examinations, the mix of yoke and coil setups and the cleaning required. We examine items against the owner's acceptance criteria; if the owner has none for NDT, a qualified person or the manufacturer can provide them, and we apply them as written.

What the report contains

  • Part identification, type, capacity markings and location, with photographs.
  • Procedure number and revision, the standard the examination follows, and the owner's specification.
  • Equipment, particles, lighting and calibration records.
  • Surface preparation and part condition, including coating, corrosion and visible wear noted but not measured.
  • Technician and level, and Level III approval of the procedure.
  • Each indication with position, orientation and length on a sketch or photograph.
  • Examination result against the named criteria, clearly separated from the decision on service status, which stays with the owner or qualified person.

What to send for a quote

  • List of items by type, quantity, rated capacity and material, with any manufacturer information.
  • The inspection standard or owner program that applies, and the frequency category (periodic, post-event or load-test preparation).
  • Whether parts will be at a yard, shop or on the crane, and who removes them from rigging.
  • Surface condition, coating and whether cleaning is included.
  • Site address, access, safety orientation and any ports, mine or plant entry requirements such as TWIC or MSHA training.

Planning on yards, docks and mines

Lifting equipment sits in steel mills, shipyards, ports, mines, power plants and construction yards. A rigging loft with a bench and power is easy. A crane on a pier or a mine haul road is not. Technicians travel to your site, and Atlantis has no office near it, so we ask about weather cover, power, a dark area for fluorescent work and lift schedules. Ports and marine terminals may require TWIC, and mining sites require federal MSHA training, so tell us before we mobilize.

Where we work in the United States

  • Houston: refinery cranes, offshore lifting gear and Ship Channel yards.
  • Gary: steel mill overhead cranes and below-the-hook devices.
  • Pittsburgh: heavy industrial lifting equipment and fabrication yards.
  • New Orleans: river and offshore lifting hardware and dock cranes.
  • Mobile: shipyard and port lifting equipment.
  • Norfolk: shipyard and terminal lifting gear.
  • Chicago: rail, steel and manufacturing cranes.
  • Birmingham: foundry, pipe and steel-plant lifting equipment.

Industry pages cover steel, offshore, marine, mining, oilfield and fabrication work. The national magnetic particle testing page lists every service location.

Training your own technicians

An owner with many hooks to examine may prefer in-house capability. Atlantis provides MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, and the company certifies its own personnel under its written practice.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform load tests, rate capacity, or return equipment to service, and crane certification is outside our scope. We do not run radiography in the United States. We report MT indications, and the owner or qualified person decides removal from service.

faq.q: Is magnetic particle inspection required on crane hooks?
faq.a: Not by every standard. ASME B30.10 and OSHA rules require periodic inspection by a qualified person, and NDT frequency is set by the owner's program, the manufacturer or that person. Many owners add MT to find cracks that a visual check could miss.

faq.q: Can you measure hook throat opening or wear?
faq.a: That is a visual and dimensional check made with gauges or calipers by the owner's inspector or qualified person. MT finds cracks; it does not measure throat spread, twist or wear, though we can note visible wear in the report.

faq.q: What do you do if you find a crack in a hook or shackle?
faq.a: We mark the indication, measure its location and length, photograph it and tell the owner's representative immediately. The owner or qualified person decides removal from service, and we do not make that call.

faq.q: Does paint have to come off before MT?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings can sometimes remain within the procedure limits, but heavy paint, rust scale and grease reduce sensitivity. The procedure states what cleaning is needed, and we agree on cleaning with you before we start.

faq.q: Can stainless steel shackles and hardware be examined by MT?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is not magnetic, so MT will not work. Liquid penetrant testing is the surface method for that hardware, and we can do it for the same site visit.

faq.q: What standards cover below-the-hook lifting devices?
faq.a: ASME B30.20 covers the use and inspection of below-the-hook lifting devices, and ASME BTH-1 sets design criteria. The owner's program decides which NDT applies, and we examine to that specification.

faq.q: Can you examine items while they are on the crane?
faq.a: Sometimes, if access, lighting and safe position allow, but many items are better examined on a bench after removal from rigging. The owner's rigging crew handles disassembly and reassembly for safety.

faq.q: What do you need to quote lifting equipment MPI?
faq.a: A list of items with type, quantity, rated capacity and material, the standard or owner program, where the parts will be, surface condition, and the site address with safety, badging or permit requirements.

No. Load testing and capacity rating are outside our scope. We examine the steel parts with magnetic particle testing and report indications; the owner arranges any proof loading through the equipment manufacturer or a qualified person.

faq.q: Is demagnetization needed after hook inspection?
faq.a: Often, since residual magnetism can attract ferrous particles and chips and affect later welding or machining. The procedure states whether demagnetization is required and how much residual field is acceptable.
